chunks: From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Bint Ilyas, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from a man, from Ali ibn Al-Husayn (peace be upon them both), who said:

"If a man makes an oath upon his brother and he does not fulfill his oath, then upon the one who made the oath is the expiation for the oath." Muhammad ibn Al-Hasan said: "This report is to be understood as indicating preference (istihbab) because we have previously presented from the reports that indicate that there is no obligation upon him."

key_terms.أَخِيهِ: his brother (often used for a fellow Muslim or close associate)
key_terms.الِاسْتِحْبَابِ: preference/recommendation (a fiqh term for a recommended but not obligatory act)
key_terms.الْقَاسِمِ: the one who made the oath

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on expiation when a man makes an oath upon his brother who fails to fulfill it?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* addresses the liability of expiation (*kaffarat al-yamin*) when an individual imposes a conditional oath upon another who subsequently fails to comply. Shaykh al-Tusi’s student, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, contextualizes this ruling as *istihbab* (recommended) rather than *wajib* (obligatory), reconciling it with other reports that suggest no penalty is due, thereby reflecting the Shia juristic principle of resolving apparent contradictions through contextual interpretation (*ta'wil*).
